content: 1. Asymptomatic excretion of immunodeficiency-related vaccine-derived poliovirus (iVDPV) is monitored by sentinel facilities, categorized by country and year. 2. Geographical distribution of primary immunodeficiency (PID) patients excreting poliovirus is mapped by country and year. 3. The age and sex distribution of PID patients with prolonged Sabin strain excretion or iVDPV excretion is analyzed. 4. PID patients diagnosed with prolonged Sabin strain excretion or iVDPV excretion are categorized based on the duration of viral shedding (prolonged versus chronic). 5. The distribution of PID patients with prolonged Sabin strain excretion or iVDPV excretion is further analyzed by their specific PID diagnosis. 6. The percentage of PID patients with prolonged Sabin strain excretion or iVDPV excretion who underwent detailed investigations, including contact tracing and community assessments, is calculated. 7. Results from contact and/or environmental sampling conducted to investigate PID patients with iVDPV excretion are reviewed. 8. The percentage of PID patients with prolonged Sabin strain excretion or iVDPV excretion who received antiviral treatment is determined. 9. The percentage of PID patients who successfully cleared poliovirus excretion following antiviral treatment is assessed. 10. The percentage of PID patients with non-polio enterovirus (NPEV) infections is documented. 11. Outcomes of cases, including continued shedding, cessation of shedding, death, or loss to follow-up, are monitored. 12. Surveillance for poliovirus excretion among PID patients is reviewed quarterly during polio eradication data review meetings, alongside data from other polio surveillance systems such as acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) and environmental surveillance (ES). 13. Data from PID surveillance is analyzed in conjunction with AFP and ES data for annual country risk assessments and reports submitted to the National Committee for the Certification of Poliomyelitis Eradication. 14. Performance indicators for PID surveillance include: Proportion of registered PID patients tested for poliovirus excretion per sentinel facility or country, with a target of >90%. Proportion of newly diagnosed PID patients tested for poliovirus excretion within the same year, with a target of >90%. Proportion of PID patients with poliovirus excretion who underwent detailed case investigations, including contact tracing and community assessments, within 48 hours of laboratory results, with a target of >80%. Proportion of specimens arriving at WHO-accredited laboratories in good condition, with a target of >80%. Proportion of specimens arriving at WHO-accredited laboratories within three days of collection, with a target of >80%. Proportion of stool specimens for which laboratory results were sent to sentinel facilities or submitting agencies within defined periods (e.g., 14 days for poliovirus isolation, 7 days for intratypic differentiation, and 7 days for sequencing results), with a target of >80%. Proportion of follow-up specimens collected out of the expected number, with a target of >80%. Proportion of active surveillance visits implemented out of the planned visits, with a target of >90%. 15. The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) was established in 1988 by the World Health Assembly to achieve polio eradication by the year 2000. At that time, over 350,000 cases of paralytic poliomyelitis were reported annually from 125 countries. 16. The last case of wild poliovirus type 2 (WPV2) was reported in October 1999 in India, and the last case of wild poliovirus type 3 (WPV3) was reported in November 2012 in Nigeria. 17. The global eradication of WPV2 was certified on 20 September 2015, and WPV3 on 24 October 2019. 18. As of October 2022, wild poliovirus type 1 (WPV1) remains endemic in only two countries: Afghanistan and Pakistan. 19. Under the International Health Regulations (IHR), the global spread of poliovirus has been declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) since 2014. The PHEIC status is reviewed every three months by the IHR Emergency Committee to assess the risk of international spread of WPV1 and circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV). 20. Polioviruses are human enteroviruses belonging to the Picornaviridae family. They are non-enveloped viruses with a single-stranded RNA genome and a protein capsid. 21. There are three serotypes of polioviruses (types 1, 2, and 3), each with distinct antigenic sites in their capsid proteins. 22. Polioviruses share most biochemical and biophysical properties with other enteroviruses. They are resistant to inactivation by many common detergents and disinfectants, including soaps, but are rapidly inactivated by ultraviolet light exposure. 23. Viral infectivity remains stable for months at +4°C and for several days at +30°C. 24. Polioviruses are transmitted via the fecal-oral and oral-oral routes. In areas with poor sanitation, fecal-oral transmission predominates, while oral-oral transmission is more common in areas with high sanitation standards. Mixed transmission patterns are likely in most settings. 25. Humans are the only known reservoir of poliovirus, and transmission occurs most frequently through individuals with inapparent infections. There is no long-term carrier state in immunocompetent hosts. 26. Poliovirus infection provides lifelong immunity against the disease, but this protection is serotype-specific. Infection with one serotype does not protect against infection with the other two serotypes. 27. The oral polio vaccine (OPV) contains live, attenuated vaccine-virus strains. When administered, the weakened vaccine-virus replicates in the intestine, enters the bloodstream, and triggers a protective immune response. The vaccine-virus is excreted in feces for six to eight weeks, during which it may undergo genetic changes, resulting in vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPVs). 28. VDPVs are classified into three categories: circulating VDPVs (cVDPVs), immunodeficiency-related VDPVs (iVDPVs), and ambiguous VDPVs (aVDPVs). 29. cVDPVs occur when excreted VDPVs circulate in under-immunized populations, potentially reacquiring neurovirulence over 12-18 months. 30. iVDPVs are observed in individuals with rare immune deficiency disorders who cannot clear intestinal vaccine-virus infections, leading to prolonged excretion. 31. aVDPVs are isolates that cannot be classified as cVDPVs or iVDPVs and may originate from individuals without known immunodeficiency or environmental samples without evidence of circulation. 32. Laboratory diagnosis of polio involves virological examination of stool samples from patients with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) to detect and characterize poliovirus. Molecular diagnostics, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), differentiate between wild poliovirus (WPV), VDPVs, and Sabin-like poliovirus. 33. Paralytic polio is a rare outcome, occurring in less than 1% of poliovirus infections, and is characterized by acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) with asymmetric, flaccid muscle weakness, fever, and rapid progression to maximum paralysis within four days. 34. Post-polio syndrome occurs in 25-50% of cases, with symptoms such as increased muscle weakness, pain, and fatigue appearing 15-30 years after recovery from the initial paralytic attack.
